title: The Moves of the Gemara: Question, Proof, Objection, Answer
bigQuestion: Why does the Talmud keep the whole argument instead of just writing down the answer?

story.title: Five Objections to One Rule
story.kicker: A seventh-grade class tries to write its own page of Talmud about phones.
paragraphs: On Monday, Ms. Rivera wrote one line on the board: "No phones in class." Then she said, "Today this is our Mishnah. Your job is to be the Gemara." The class looked at her. Deshawn raised his hand first. "What counts as a phone?" he asked. "Is a smartwatch a phone?" Ms. Rivera wrote his question under the rule and labeled it Question.

Maya offered a proof. "The school handbook says no devices that can send messages. A smartwatch can send messages. So it counts." Ms. Rivera wrote that down as Proof. Then Omar objected. "But the handbook also lets students use a calculator. Some calculators have screens too." The room got louder. Ms. Rivera smiled and wrote Objection.

By the end of the period the board was full. There were five objections. One asked about a student who needs a phone to check blood sugar. Another asked about an emergency call from home. The class agreed that the rule must bend to protect health and safety. They did not agree about the smartwatch, so Ms. Rivera wrote one word next to it: teyku, "let it stand."

"Now look," she said. "If I erased everything but the answer, what would you lose?" Priya said, "We would lose why." Ms. Rivera nodded. "The Talmud keeps the why. That is what we will study this week."
story.think: Which part of the class's board would help most if a new question came up next year: the final answer or the argument? Why?

lessons.title: A Unit of Discussion
lessons.mainIdea: A sugya is one complete discussion in the Gemara, and it usually moves through question, proof, objection and answer.
reading: Open the Babylonian Talmud to Berakhot 2a, the first page of the first tractate. The Mishnah asks a plain question: from what time may the evening Shema be said? Right after it, the Gemara begins its own discussion. That discussion, from its first question to its last answer, is called a *sugya*.

Scholars describe a sugya as a unit of argument. It often starts with a Mishnah. Then a rabbi asks about it. Someone brings a proof. Someone else raises an objection. The discussion ends with an answer, or sometimes with no answer at all. A single page can hold several sugyot, and one sugya can run for many pages.

The word sugya comes from Aramaic and is often explained as "a going" or "a path." Teachers like that meaning. A sugya is a path the reader walks, step by step. Learning Talmud, many teachers say, means learning to walk that path and see where each step leads.

words.d: one complete discussion in the Gemara, from its opening question to its end; plural sugyot
the rabbis' recorded discussion of the Mishnah, written mostly in Aramaic

look.title: Mapping the Steps
look.text: Step 1: a Mishnah states a rule. Step 2: a rabbi asks, "What is the reason?" Step 3: another rabbi quotes a verse as proof. Step 4: someone objects that the verse could mean something else. Step 5: an answer explains why the verse still works.
look.prompt: Label each step with one word: rule, question, proof, objection or answer. Which step do you think takes the most skill?

check.q: What is a sugya?
choices: One complete discussion in the Gemara
A single verse from the Torah
A commentary printed in the margin
check.why: A sugya is one unit of discussion in the Gemara, from its first question to its end.

check.q: Where does a sugya very often begin?
check.why: Many sugyot start from a Mishnah and then ask about it.

check.q: Why do teachers like the meaning "a path" for sugya?
choices: A sugya is about travel laws only
A sugya is always one line long
A sugya moves step by step, like walking a path
A sugya is written as a map
check.why: The idea of a path fits how a sugya moves from one step of the argument to the next.

lessons.title: What Is the Reason?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara often opens by asking "mai ta'ama?" (what is the reason?), because it wants to know why a rule is true, not only what it says.
reading: Again and again the Gemara asks two Aramaic words: *mai ta'ama*, "what is the reason?" A Mishnah may state a rule in one short line. The Gemara wants to know what stands behind it. Is it a verse from the Torah? Is it a teaching from an earlier rabbi? Is it common sense?

Knowing the reason matters for new cases. Suppose a rule says a finder must announce a lost coat. If the reason is that the owner can prove the coat is theirs by a mark, then the rule might change for an object with no mark. The Gemara reasons this way in Bava Metzia, the tractate about lost objects and business.

So the question "what is the reason?" is not rude. In the Talmud it is a sign of respect for the rule. The rabbis treat a rule as something that can be understood. Once they understand it, they can apply it to cases the Mishnah never mentioned.

words.d: Aramaic for "what is the reason?"; a common question in the Gemara
"the middle gate"; a tractate about lost objects, loans, workers and business

look.title: Same Rule, New Case
look.text: Rule: If you find something with a mark on it, announce it so the owner can claim it. New case: you find a plain pencil with no mark, in a busy hallway.
look.prompt: If the reason for the rule is "the owner can prove it by the mark," what should happen with the plain pencil? Explain your step.

check.q: What does mai ta'ama mean?
choices: From the lighter to the heavier
check.why: Mai ta'ama is Aramaic for "what is the reason?"

check.q: Why does knowing a rule's reason help with new cases?
choices: The reason shows when the rule does or does not apply
The reason tells you which page the rule is on
The reason makes the rule shorter
The reason is needed only for prayers
check.why: If you know why a rule exists, you can decide whether it fits a case the Mishnah never mentioned.

check.q: Which tractate deals with lost objects?
check.why: Bava Metzia, "the middle gate," deals with lost objects, loans and workers.

lessons.title: Proof from a Verse
lessons.mainIdea: A common move in the Gemara is to support a rule with a verse from the Hebrew Bible.
reading: On Berakhot 2a the Gemara asks why the Mishnah speaks of the evening Shema before the morning one. Its first answer points to a verse. Deuteronomy 6:7 says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Lying down comes first in the verse, so evening comes first in the Mishnah.

Then the Gemara offers a second answer. Genesis 1:5 describes creation with the words "there was evening and there was morning." In the order of creation, too, evening comes before morning. The Gemara keeps both answers side by side. It does not erase the first when it finds the second.

A proof from a verse is a basic move in the Talmud. Rabbinic tradition holds that the Written Torah and the rabbis' teaching fit together. So a rabbi who wants to support a rule often looks for words in the Bible that point to it. Other rabbis then test the proof to see if the verse really says what is claimed.

words.d: a verse or teaching brought to support a claim in the Gemara
the declaration beginning "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4), said in the evening and morning in Jewish practice

look.title: Why Evening First?
look.text: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah starts with the evening Shema. One answer: the verse says "when you lie down" before "when you rise up." Another answer: in the creation story, evening comes before morning.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 2a (paraphrase; see William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria, 2017); verses from JPS Tanakh (1917), Deuteronomy 6:7 and Genesis 1:5
look.prompt: The Gemara gives two different proofs for the same rule. Why might it keep both instead of choosing one?

check.q: On Berakhot 2a, what does the Gemara want to explain?
choices: Why the Mishnah mentions the evening Shema first
How to return a lost coat
check.why: Berakhot 2a asks why the Mishnah begins with the evening Shema rather than the morning one.

check.q: Which verse does the Gemara use to show that evening comes first in creation?
check.why: Genesis 1:5 describes evening and then morning, and the Gemara uses it as a second proof.

check.q: What happens to a proof after a rabbi offers it?
choices: Other rabbis test it to see if it really works
It is printed in red ink
check.why: In the Gemara, proofs are tested by objections; that testing is what moves the sugya forward.

lessons.title: The Kushya
lessons.mainIdea: A kushya is an objection or difficulty, and raising one is how the Gemara tests every claim.
reading: In the Gemara, a claim is never safe just because a great rabbi said it. Someone may point out a problem. The problem might be a verse that seems to say the opposite. It might be a Mishnah that disagrees. It might be a case where the claim gives a strange result. That problem is called a *kushya*, a difficulty or objection.

The Gemara has set phrases for objections. One is "meitivi," meaning "they raised an objection." Another is "ve-ha-tanya," "but was it not taught…?" These phrases tell the reader that a challenge is coming. Students learn to spot them, because they mark a turn in the path.

Teachers who run a *chavruta*, a study pair, often tell students to play the objector on purpose. One partner reads a claim. The other looks for the kushya. Many readers of the Talmud say this is not about winning. A claim that has faced hard objections and survived is a claim you can trust more.

words.d: an objection or difficulty raised against a claim in the Gemara
a pair of study partners who read and argue through a text together

look.title: Find the Difficulty
look.text: Claim: "Students may leave class early if they finish the test." Another school rule says: "Students must stay in the room until the bell during testing."
look.prompt: State the kushya in one sentence. Then suggest one way someone could answer it.

check.q: What is a kushya?
check.why: A kushya is a difficulty raised against a claim.

check.q: What does the phrase "meitivi" tell a reader?
choices: A story is about to begin
check.why: Meitivi means "they raised an objection" and signals a challenge.

check.q: Why do many teachers want students in chavruta to raise objections?
choices: Objections end the study session early
Only one partner is allowed to speak
A claim that survives hard objections can be trusted more
check.why: Testing a claim with objections shows whether it holds up.

lessons.title: The Terutz
lessons.mainIdea: A terutz is an answer that resolves an objection, often by showing that two sources speak about different cases.
reading: After a kushya comes the search for a *terutz*, an answer. One of the most common kinds of answer is a split between cases. The Gemara says, in effect, "This source is talking about one situation, and that source is talking about another." Suddenly two texts that seemed to clash can both be true.

Here is how that looks. Suppose one teaching says a worker may eat from the crop he harvests. Another seems to say he may not. The Gemara might answer that one teaching speaks while he is working and the other speaks after he has finished. The Mishnah in Bava Metzia 7:2 does draw lines like these about when a worker may eat.

Some answers are strong. Others the Gemara itself calls weak or forced. Rabbinic readers and modern scholars both notice this. The Talmud does not pretend every answer is equally good. It often signals when an answer is only a way to keep a view alive.

words.d: an answer that resolves an objection in the Gemara
the early rabbinic law code, arranged c. 200 CE, written mostly in Hebrew

look.title: When a Worker May Eat
look.text: The Mishnah says a field worker may eat from the crop while he is harvesting it, as the Torah allows, but not from a crop he is not working on. It lists which workers and which moments count.
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:2 (paraphrase; see Herbert Danby, The Mishnah, 1933); based on Deuteronomy 23:25–26, JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: How does splitting "while working" from "not working" help protect both the worker and the owner?

check.q: What is a terutz?
check.why: A terutz answers a kushya, the objection.

check.q: What is a common way the Gemara answers two sources that seem to clash?
choices: It shows they speak about different cases
It asks the reader to vote
check.why: Splitting the cases lets both sources stand.

check.q: According to Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:2, when may a field worker eat from the crop?
check.why: The Mishnah allows a worker to eat from the crop he is working on.

lessons.title: Teyku: Let It Stand
lessons.mainIdea: Sometimes the Gemara ends a question with teyku, "let it stand," and leaves it unresolved.
reading: Not every sugya ends with a neat answer. Sometimes the rabbis ask a question, try several answers, and none of them works. Then the Gemara writes one word: *teyku*. It means "let it stand." The question stays open.

Many teyku questions are detailed puzzles about unusual cases. The Gemara in Bava Metzia, for example, raises cases about lost objects and ownership that it cannot settle. A later popular tradition reads the letters of teyku as a short form of a Hebrew phrase: Elijah the prophet will one day answer the questions. Scholars note that this reading came later; the word itself simply means the question stands.

Teyku teaches something about the Talmud's stance. The rabbis were willing to write down what they did not know. They did not hide an open question to look wise. For students, teyku is a model of honest study: say what the evidence shows, and admit where it runs out.

words.d: "let it stand"; the Gemara's word for a question left unresolved
a biblical prophet who, in later Jewish tradition, will one day settle open questions

look.title: Two Endings
look.text: Ending A: "The answer is yes, because of the verse." Ending B: "We tried three answers and each one had a problem. Teyku."
look.prompt: Which ending tells a future reader more about the question? Give one reason.

check.q: What does teyku mean?
choices: From the lighter to the heavier
check.why: Teyku means "let it stand"; the question stays open.

check.q: According to a later popular tradition, who will one day answer the teyku questions?
check.why: A later tradition reads teyku as pointing to Elijah, who will settle open questions; scholars say the reading came later.

check.q: What does teyku show about the rabbis' way of study?
choices: They wrote down honestly what they could not settle
check.why: Recording an unresolved question shows honesty about the limits of an argument.

lessons.title: From Light to Heavy
lessons.mainIdea: Kal va-chomer is an argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if a rule holds in the easy case, it holds even more in the hard case.
reading: *Kal va-chomer* means "light and heavy." It is an argument from the smaller case to the bigger one. If a rule is true where it matters less, it must be true where it matters more. English speakers call this an argument a fortiori.

Rabbinic tradition finds examples in the Torah itself. In Numbers 12:14, after Miriam is struck with a skin disease, God tells Moses that if her father had spit in her face, she would hide in shame seven days. How much more, the verse implies, should she be shut out after this. The Gemara in Bava Kamma 25a points to this verse as a model of kal va-chomer.

Kal va-chomer appears among the seven rules of reasoning linked with Hillel, who taught around the turn of the Common Era. Later lists expanded them to thirteen, linked with Rabbi Ishmael. The rabbis also knew the tool's limits. A kal va-chomer can be refuted if someone shows that the "light" case has a feature the "heavy" case lacks.

words.d: "light and heavy"; an argument from a lesser case to a greater one
Latin for "from the stronger"; the English name for the same kind of argument
a sage who taught in Jerusalem around the turn of the Common Era; tradition links seven rules of reasoning with him

look.title: Build One
look.text: Fact: Students are asked to be quiet in the hallway during tests. Question: What about inside the testing room itself?
look.prompt: Write the kal va-chomer: "If ___, then how much more ___." Then name one way someone could object.

check.q: What kind of argument is kal va-chomer?
choices: An argument from a matching word in two verses
An argument from a lesser case to a greater one
A story told to teach a lesson
check.why: Kal va-chomer argues that what holds in the lighter case holds all the more in the heavier.

check.q: Which verse does Bava Kamma 25a use as a model of kal va-chomer?
check.why: The Gemara points to the Miriam verse, where "if her father had spit… how much more" is implied.

check.q: How can a kal va-chomer be refuted?
choices: By showing the light case has a feature the heavy case lacks
check.why: If the lighter case has something special, the argument no longer carries over.

lessons.title: A Matching Word
lessons.mainIdea: Gezerah shavah links two laws because the Torah uses the same word in both places.
reading: *Gezerah shavah* means "an equal decree." It connects two passages of the Torah that share a word or phrase. What is clear in one passage is then carried over to the other. It is another of the rules of reasoning linked with Hillel.

The Gemara in Pesachim 66a tells a famous story. One year the eve of Passover fell on the Sabbath. The leaders did not know if the Passover offering could be made that day. Hillel argued that the daily Temple offering is made on the Sabbath, and the Torah uses the phrase "in its appointed season" for both offerings. So the Passover offering, too, could be made on the Sabbath.

The rabbis were careful with this tool. The Gemara teaches that a person may not invent a gezerah shavah on their own; it must be received from a teacher. Rabbinic readers explain that this rule kept the tool from being used to prove anything at all. It shows the rabbis thinking about the limits of their own methods.

words.d: "an equal decree"; linking two laws because the Torah uses the same word in both
"Passover offerings"; the tractate about Passover

look.title: Hillel and the Sabbath Eve
look.text: The sages asked if the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath. Hillel answered that the Torah says "in its appointed season" about the Passover offering and also about the daily offering. Since the daily offering is brought on the Sabbath, so is the Passover offering.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 66a (paraphrase; see William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria, 2017); phrase from Numbers 9:2 and 28:2, JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: What is the shared phrase in Hillel's argument, and what does it let him carry from one law to the other?

check.q: What links two laws in a gezerah shavah?
choices: One law is lighter than the other
The same word or phrase appears in both passages
Both are in the same tractate
check.why: A gezerah shavah connects passages that share a word or phrase.

check.q: In Pesachim 66a, what question did Hillel answer?
choices: Whether a worker may eat from the field
Why the evening Shema comes first
Whether the Passover offering may be made on the Sabbath
check.why: The story tells how Hillel showed the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath.

check.q: Why did the rabbis say a gezerah shavah must come from a teacher?
choices: Because the word was in Aramaic
Because it was a secret prayer
To keep the tool from being used to prove anything at all
check.why: Rabbinic readers explain the limit as a guard against misuse.

lessons.title: A Teaching from Outside
lessons.mainIdea: A baraita is a teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was left out of it, and the Gemara often quotes one as a proof or an objection.
reading: The rabbis of the Mishnah are called *tannaim*, "repeaters" or teachers. The rabbis of the Gemara are called *amoraim*, "speakers" or explainers. The Mishnah did not hold everything the tannaim taught. Teachings left outside it are called *baraitot*, from an Aramaic word for "outside."

In the Gemara a baraita is often introduced by "tanu rabbanan," "our rabbis taught," or "tanya," "it was taught." A baraita carries weight because it comes from the earlier generation. So when an amora makes a claim, another amora may quote a baraita against it. That is a strong objection.

The answer sometimes becomes one of the most common moves in the Talmud: the baraita and the claim speak about different cases. Readers learn to ask of every quotation, "Who is speaking here, a tanna or an amora?" The answer tells you how much authority the words carry in the argument.

words.d: a teaching of the tannaim left outside the Mishnah; plural baraitot
a rabbi of the Mishnah's time, up to about 200 CE; plural tannaim
a rabbi of the Gemara's time, about 200 to 500 CE; plural amoraim

look.title: Who Speaks When
look.cite: Common scholarly dating; see Hermann L. Strack and Günter Stemberger, Introduction to the Talmud and Midrash (1991)
look.prompt: About how many years separate the end of the tannaim from Abaye and Rava? Why does that gap make a baraita a strong proof?

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A teaching of the tannaim left outside the Mishnah
check.why: A baraita is an early teaching that was not included in the Mishnah.

check.q: Which phrase often introduces a baraita?
check.why: Tanu rabbanan signals a teaching from the tannaim.

check.q: Who are the amoraim?
choices: The rabbis of the Mishnah's time
The printers of the Vilna page
The rabbis of the Gemara's time
check.why: The amoraim, c. 200–500 CE, discussed the Mishnah in the Gemara.

lessons.title: Rav and Shmuel
lessons.mainIdea: Rav and Shmuel were early amoraim in Babylonia whose disagreements run through the Talmud.
reading: In the early 200s CE, a rabbi called Rav came to Babylonia from the Land of Israel. Tradition says he founded an academy at Sura. His colleague Shmuel led the Jewish community's learning at Nehardea. Both belong to the first generation of Babylonian amoraim.

The Gemara often sets their views side by side: "Rav said… and Shmuel said…" Rabbinic tradition sums up a pattern. In matters of ritual law the ruling usually follows Rav. In matters of civil law, such as money and damages, it usually follows Shmuel. Shmuel was also known for skill in astronomy and medicine.

Shmuel is also linked with a famous principle, found in several tractates: "the law of the kingdom is the law." It means Jews should follow the fair civil laws of the country where they live. Readers across the centuries have discussed how far that principle reaches.

words.d: a first-generation Babylonian amora (early 200s CE) linked by tradition with the academy at Sura
a first-generation Babylonian amora at Nehardea, known for civil law and astronomy

look.title: Two Voices, Two Areas
look.text: Case A: a question about the right time for a blessing. Case B: a question about who pays when a borrowed tool breaks.
look.prompt: According to the traditional pattern, whose view would usually decide each case? What might explain a pattern like that?

check.q: Where did Rav found an academy, according to tradition?
check.why: Tradition says Rav founded the academy at Sura in Babylonia.

check.q: In the traditional pattern, the ruling in civil law usually follows whom?
check.why: Rabbinic tradition says civil law usually follows Shmuel, ritual law usually Rav.

check.q: What does "the law of the kingdom is the law" mean?
choices: Jews should follow the fair civil laws of the country where they live
The Talmud must be printed by a king
Every ruling is made by vote
check.why: The principle, linked with Shmuel, treats fair local civil law as binding in civil matters.

lessons.title: Abaye and Rava
lessons.mainIdea: Abaye and Rava were fourth-century amoraim whose debates became a symbol of Talmud study itself.
reading: About a hundred years after Rav and Shmuel, two more rabbis became famous as a pair. Abaye led the academy at Pumbedita. Rava taught at Mahoza. Both lived in the 300s CE. Their debates fill so many pages that "the discussions of Abaye and Rava" became a way to describe Talmud learning.

In most of their disputes the halakhah, Jewish law as the Talmud develops it, follows Rava. The Gemara in Bava Metzia 22b lists six exceptions where it follows Abaye. Students remember the six by a memory word, Ya'al Kegam, made from the first letters of the six cases.

The pair is a good example of how the Talmud treats the side that did not win. Abaye's arguments are kept in full. Students study them as carefully as Rava's. A learner cannot understand Rava's answer without knowing what Abaye asked.

words.d: Jewish law as the Talmud and later teachers develop it
a fourth-century Babylonian amora who led the academy at Pumbedita
a fourth-century Babylonian amora at Mahoza, Abaye's frequent partner in debate

look.title: Rulings Between Two Rabbis
rows: Cases where the law follows Abaye
Letters in the memory word Ya'al Kegam
Generations of amoraim in Babylonia, a common count
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 22b; generation count from common scholarly lists (counts vary)
look.prompt: Why would students need a memory word for six exceptions instead of a list of every case Rava won?

check.q: In most disputes between Abaye and Rava, whom does the halakhah follow?
check.why: The rule is that the law follows Rava, except in six cases.

check.q: What is Ya'al Kegam?
choices: A memory word for the six cases where the law follows Abaye
check.why: Ya'al Kegam is built from the first letters of the six cases, listed in Bava Metzia 22b.

check.q: Why do students still study Abaye's side?
choices: Rava's answer cannot be understood without Abaye's question
Abaye's view is always the law
check.why: The Talmud keeps both sides because each argument depends on the other.

lessons.title: Why the Minority Is Kept
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah and the Gemara record views that lost, and they give reasons for doing so.
reading: Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 asks a sharp question. If the law follows the majority, why write down the view of a single rabbi who was outvoted? Its answer: so that a later court, if it sees reason, may rely on that view. A minority opinion is saved for a future that may need it.

The Gemara in Eruvin 13b tells of a three-year dispute between the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai. A heavenly voice declares that both views are "the words of the living God," and that the law follows Hillel's house. Why Hillel's? The Gemara says they were kind and humble, and they taught Shammai's view before their own.

Readers have taken this in different ways. Orthodox teachers often stress that both sides were seeking truth within the tradition. Reform and Conservative teachers often point to it as a model for respectful disagreement. Academic scholars study how the editors shaped the story. All of them notice that the Talmud keeps the losing side.

words.d: a view that was not followed as law but is still recorded in the text
the school of Hillel's students; the Talmud usually rules with them against the House of Shammai

look.title: Both Are Words of the Living God
look.text: After three years of dispute, a heavenly voice declares that the words of both the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai are words of the living God, but the law follows the House of Hillel. The Gemara explains: they were gentle and humble, and taught the other side's words, even putting them first.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (paraphrase; see William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: According to this passage, why did Hillel's house win? What does that suggest about how the Gemara values the way people argue?

check.q: According to Mishnah Eduyot 1:5, why is a lone rabbi's view recorded?
choices: To show that he was wrong forever
So a later court may rely on it if it sees reason
Because every view is the law
check.why: Eduyot 1:5 says a minority view is kept so a later court can rely on it.

check.q: In Eruvin 13b, why does the law follow the House of Hillel?
choices: They were kind and humble and taught Shammai's view first
The House of Shammai left no teachings
check.why: The Gemara ties the ruling to the House of Hillel's humility and fairness.

check.q: Which statement describes the readers of Eruvin 13b fairly?
choices: Only one group of Jews reads it
Scholars say the story never mentions Shammai
All readers agree on exactly one meaning
Different Jewish groups read it in different ways, and all notice the losing side is kept
check.why: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers stress different points in the same passage.

review.why: A sugya typically moves from a question to a proof, then an objection and an answer.

review.q: A rabbi says a rule holds even more strongly in a bigger case. Which tool is that?
review.why: Kal va-chomer argues from the lighter case to the heavier one.

review.q: Which word marks a question the Gemara leaves unresolved?
What is the difference between a tanna and an amora?
choices: A tanna wrote in the margin; an amora printed the page
A tanna is a question; an amora is an answer
A tanna taught in the Mishnah's time; an amora taught in the Gemara's time
review.why: Tannaim are the Mishnah's teachers; amoraim, later, discussed the Mishnah.

review.q: Hillel's argument in Pesachim 66a used a phrase found in two laws. What tool is that?
review.why: Linking two laws by a shared phrase is a gezerah shavah.

review.q: Which pair of amoraim led academies at Pumbedita and Mahoza in the 300s CE?
review.why: Abaye led Pumbedita and Rava taught at Mahoza.

review.q: In Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:2, whom does the rule about eating from the crop protect?
choices: The worker, and also the owner, by setting limits
No one; it is a story
review.why: The rule lets a worker eat while harvesting and sets limits that protect the owner.

review.q: What reason does Eruvin 13b give for the law following the House of Hillel?
review.why: The Gemara says the House of Hillel was gentle and humble and taught the other side first.
